clinicalPearls: A common cause of chronic axial (midline) mechanical low back or neck pain without radiculopathy
Pain is typically worse with sitting, bending, lifting, and axial loading, and is eased by lying down
Reflects age-related disc dehydration and degeneration rather than a discrete disease, and imaging changes are extremely common in asymptomatic people
MRI shows loss of disc signal (a dark disc), reduced disc height, and vertebral endplate (Modic) changes
Endplate Modic changes, particularly type 1, may correlate with a painful disc
The diagnosis is clinical, and the correlation between imaging degeneration and pain is weak, so imaging must be interpreted cautiously
Management is predominantly conservative, including education, exercise and physiotherapy, analgesia, and weight management
Fusion or disc replacement is controversial and reserved for carefully selected patients with disabling, single-level discogenic pain unresponsive to prolonged conservative care
reference.pathophysiology: Degenerative disc disease describes the symptomatic consequences of intervertebral disc ageing. Progressive loss of proteoglycan and water content reduces the disc's ability to distribute load, leading to disc-height loss, annular fissuring, and altered biomechanics. Pain is thought to arise from stimulation of nociceptors in the outer annulus and vertebral endplates, sometimes accompanied by ingrowth of nerves and blood vessels into the degenerate disc and by inflammatory endplate (Modic) changes. Because degeneration is almost universal with age, structural changes correlate poorly with symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in younger patients with inflammatory features
Metastatic or infective spinal disease when red flags are present
additionalInvestigations: MRI to assess disc hydration, height, and endplate (Modic) changes
Plain radiographs including standing views for disc-space narrowing and alignment
Bone density assessment if an osteoporotic fracture is a consideration
Inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 if spondyloarthropathy is suspected
Provocative discography only in highly selected surgical candidates, and even then controversially
redFlags: Constitutional symptoms, night pain, or a history of malignancy suggesting tumour
Fever or features suggesting discitis or osteomyelitis
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to fluctuate but is usually self-limiting or manageable over the long term with conservative measures; most people do not require surgery, and surgical outcomes for axial discogenic pain are less predictable than for radicular symptoms.
pitfalls: Over-interpreting ubiquitous age-related disc changes on MRI as the definite pain source
Recommending fusion for poorly localised, multilevel degeneration
Neglecting psychosocial contributors to chronic back pain
references: NICE guideline: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s
management: First-line conservative management with reassurance, education, activity modification and avoidance of prolonged bed rest, since most axial discogenic pain is self-limiting
Structured physiotherapy with core stabilisation and graded exercise to improve function and reduce mechanical pain
Analgesia using simple analgesics and short courses of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, with neuropathic agents or muscle relaxants as adjuncts where appropriate
Lifestyle measures including weight management, smoking cessation (smoking accelerates disc degeneration) and ergonomic and postural advice
Multidisciplinary chronic-pain management with psychological approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy for persistent disabling pain
Cautious interpretation of imaging and avoidance of over-investigation given the weak correlation between degenerative changes and symptoms
Reserve interventional injections and spinal fusion or disc arthroplasty for carefully selected patients with refractory, well-localised discogenic pain, with specialist spinal referral
